strengths: Principled and training-free approach: Adapting Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) to steer autoregressive music generation provides a parameter-efficient, backpropagation-free mechanism for fine-grained musical attribute control without altering base model weights.

Audio-domain specific adaptations: The paper introduces several effective adaptations over text-based activation steering, including mean-pooling representations across sequence length, layer-wise exponential weighting based on probe validation, and Bernoulli stochastic gating to prevent generative collapse and audio quality degradation.

Broad exploration of music-theoretic concepts: The method is evaluated across a wide spectrum of musical features from the SYNTHEORY benchmark (notes, intervals, scales, chords, progressions, tempo, time signatures), as well as real-world music data (MUSICBENCH).

Creative and practical control mechanisms: Demonstrating time-dependent scheduling (linear/exponential decay, sinusoidal modulation) and smooth concept cross-fading highlights compelling real-world applications for interactive music composition.

Comprehensive evaluation: The authors validate the method using diverse metrics, including distributional similarity (FD, MMD), prompt adherence (CLAP), external MIR tool evaluators (Essentia chord estimation, librosa onset detection), and a subjective listening test.
weaknesses: Missing comparisons to standard activation steering baselines: While the paper compares against prompt-based conditioning and FFN probes, it lacks comparisons against established activation-space steering methods such as Activation Addition (ActAdd), Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), or simple difference-in-means/PCA vectors. It is therefore difficult to isolate how much of the steering efficacy is uniquely attributable to RFM's AGOP versus standard linear steering vectors.

Limited efficacy on sequential and complex musical concepts: The controllability gains are heavily skewed towards local/static concepts (single notes and chords), whereas sequential and structure-heavy concepts (chord progressions, scales, time signatures) show modest improvements, likely due to mean-pooling over time.

Scale of human evaluation: The listening test involves only 12 participants evaluating 24 audio samples, which is relatively small to draw statistically robust conclusions across the diverse set of musical attributes tested.

strengths: Principled adaptation of Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) to autoregressive music generation (MusicGen-Large), offering backpropagation-free, inference-time activation steering without modifying or retraining base model weights.

Well-motivated domain-specific architectural adjustments, including mean-pooled representations over audio tokens, validation-based layer pruning (top-K and exponential weighting), and stochastic Bernoulli injection to mitigate generation drift.

Comprehensive exploration of dynamic controllability, including continuous temporal schedules (linear, logistic, exponential, sinusoidal), smooth crossfading between musical concepts, and simultaneous multi-direction steering.

Multi-faceted evaluation combining generative distributional metrics (FD, MMD), prompt alignment (CLAP), internal probe accuracy, external MIR evaluators (chromagrams, Essentia chord extraction, onset density), and a subjective listening test.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in using RFM probes to evaluate RFM steering in the main tables (Table 2 and Table 6); while external evaluators in Table 4 help validate note and tempo steering, external chord dominance remains relatively low (~30-35%) and indicates that steering higher-level harmonic structures remains challenging.

Noticeable quality degradation and distributional drift (steep increases in FD and MMD, and drops in CLAP score) at higher steering strengths (η0 ≥ 0.45) and especially in multi-direction steering scenarios.

Mean-pooling feature extraction inherently collapses temporal order, leading to limited steerability on sequentially structured music-theoretic concepts such as chord progressions, scales, and time signatures.
The human listening study is relatively small in scale (12 participants evaluating 24 audio clips total), providing helpful initial evidence but limited statistical power.

strengths: Novel application of Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) and activation-space steering to autoregressive music generation (MusicGen-Large), offering an inference-time, training-free alternative to costly fine-tuning or per-step optimization.

Thoughtful domain-specific adaptations for audio, including mean-pooling representations over time instead of last-token pooling, selective layer weighting (exponential/top-K pruning), and stochastic Bernoulli injection to mitigate representation drift.
Support for continuous, dynamic temporal control (e.g., linear ramps, sinusoidal modulation, and smooth crossfades between pitch classes) without retraining the underlying foundation model.
Comprehensive ablations evaluating the impact of layer pruning, injection schedules, and probability gating on Fréchet Distance, MMD, and CLAP alignment.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in quantitative evaluation: The main metric for steering success across many categories in Tables 2, 5, and 6 is probe accuracy evaluated by multiclass RFM probes trained on the same feature representations and synthetic dataset, which may artificially inflate steering metrics.

Modest controllability on complex musical attributes: While single-note steering shows prominent gains, more complex music-theoretic concepts (such as chord progressions, scales, and time signatures) show marginal improvements over random baseline (e.g., progression accuracy improves only from 5.3% chance to 11.4% in Table 2, and real-music tempo regression largely fails with MSE 0.862).

Severe quality and alignment trade-offs in multi-direction steering: Enforcing multiple attributes simultaneously leads to drastic degradation in audio distribution and prompt adherence (CLAP score plummets from ~0.33 to ~0.13, while FD and MMD increase by orders of magnitude in Table 6).

Limited subjective evaluation: The human listening test is underpowered, relying on only 12 participants from a single computer science department rating 24 total audio samples across four control types, which weakens confidence in the statistical significance of perceptual findings.

strengths: Novel application of Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) and Average Gradient Outer Product (AGOP) analysis to activation-space steering in autoregressive music generation (MusicGen-Large).

Well-motivated domain-specific enhancements for audio steering, including mean-pooled representations over sequence length, probe-score-based layer weighting/pruning, stochastic Bernoulli injection, and continuous temporal scheduling.
Comprehensive exploration of diverse music-theoretic properties (pitches, chords, intervals, tempo, scales) across both synthetic benchmark data (SYNTHEORY) and real-world audio (MusicBench).
Demonstration of practical creative workflows, such as multi-attribute steering, dynamic temporal modulation (e.g., sine waves, logistic rise), and smooth cross-fading between musical concepts.
weaknesses: Reliance on probe-based metrics for measuring controllability: In Tables 2 and 5, steering effectiveness is primarily evaluated using the multiclass RFM probes trained on the same representations. While the authors acknowledge this limitation in Section 5.2, validating generations with established, independent Music Information Retrieval (MIR) tools (e.g., CREPE/pYIN for pitch/notes, Madmom/Essentia for tempo and chord recognition) would provide more objective proof of musical adherence.

Lack of non-RFM activation steering baselines: The experiments compare MusicRFM against unsteered baselines and 'Naïve RFM', but omit common activation engineering techniques from the literature, such as Activation Addition (ActAdd), Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), or steering vectors derived from standard linear probes / difference-of-means.

Significant trade-off between control strength and generative fidelity: In the multi-direction steering experiments (Table 5) and higher single-direction coefficients (Table 2), distributional metrics (FD, MMD) worsen markedly and CLAP text alignment drops substantially (e.g., falling from ~0.32 to ~0.13 in Table 5), suggesting notable out-of-distribution distortion when enforcing stronger constraints.

Small-scale subjective evaluation: The listening test relies on only 12 participants evaluating 3 clips across 4 control types, and evaluates audio quality and adherence in a single combined metric rather than reporting them separately.

strengths: The application of activation-space steering via Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) to autoregressive music models (MusicGen) is timely and conceptually appealing, avoiding computationally expensive finetuning or per-step optimization.

The paper introduces thoughtful domain-specific extensions, including mean-pooled representations over sequence tokens, layer-wise weighting/pruning, stochastic Bernoulli injection, and time-varying schedules (e.g., fades and crossfades).

The manuscript is well-structured, clearly written, and covers a wide breadth of experiments, including single-direction steering, multi-direction joint steering, temporal crossfading, real-data validation on MusicBench, and detailed ablations in the appendix.
weaknesses: A major limitation is the reliance on RFM probes to evaluate steering success (Probe Acc in Tables 2, 4, 5). Steering activations along a direction derived from an RFM probe will naturally bias representations to score higher under that same probe family. Validating musical adherence with standard, external Music Information Retrieval (MIR) tools (such as CREPE/basic-pitch for notes, madmom for tempo/beats, or Chordino for chords) would provide much more objective and convincing proof of control.

Lack of comparison to established activation steering baselines. The paper only compares MusicRFM against 'No Steering' and 'Naïve RFM'. Standard activation engineering techniques such as Activation Addition (ActAdd / mean-difference vectors) or linear probe normal vectors should be compared to demonstrate whether the iterative AGOP computation of RFMs provides tangible benefits over simpler steering vectors.

The human evaluation is quite small in scale (12 participants evaluating only 3 audio samples across 4 attributes) and lacks statistical rigor or detailed reporting of questionnaire protocol and scoring scales (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS standards).

Controllability on complex, sequential musical concepts (such as chord progressions, scales, and intervals) remains quite weak (probe accuracies hovering between 0.11 and 0.25 in Table 2), which limits the practical applicability primarily to static single-note biasing.

strengths: Interesting application of Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) to activation-space steering in frozen autoregressive text-to-music models (MusicGen), avoiding costly fine-tuning or per-step optimization.
Thoughtful domain-specific stabilization heuristics, including layer weighting/pruning, Bernoulli stochastic injection, and time-dependent schedules (e.g., cross-fading and smooth modulations).
Comprehensive exploration across multiple music-theoretic dimensions (notes, intervals, scales, chords, progressions, time signatures, tempos) alongside ablation studies on injection parameters.
weaknesses: Circular and unvalidated evaluation of controllability: The primary quantitative measure of whether a generation follows the target attribute is classification accuracy under the authors' own internal RFM probes. Testing whether injecting an RFM-derived vector increases the score of an RFM probe is largely self-referential. Standard objective music information retrieval (MIR) tools (e.g., CREPE/basic-pitch for pitch/notes, Madmom/Essentia for tempo and chord recognition) are completely absent.

Missing steering baselines: The paper does not compare RFM steering against established activation engineering baselines, such as Activation Addition (ActAdd), Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), or simple difference-in-means vectors. Without these comparisons, it is impossible to assess whether the AGOP/RFM machinery offers practical benefits over much simpler linear direction extraction methods.

Poor controllability on complex and sequential musical concepts: Except for isolated single notes (which reach 0.824), accuracy for all other musical attributes remains extremely low (e.g., progressions at 0.114, scales at 0.176, chords at 0.344, intervals at 0.223). Global mean-pooling across temporal tokens fundamentally washes out sequential structures (such as chord progressions and time signatures), making the approach ill-suited for time-varying harmonic concepts.

Severely underpowered human evaluation: The listening test involves only 12 participants evaluating 3 audio samples across 4 control categories. This sample size is far too small to draw statistically significant conclusions regarding audio fidelity or attribute adherence.

Sharp fidelity degradation under stronger steering: In multi-direction steering and real-music benchmarks (MusicBench), increasing the steering coefficient leads to substantial distributional drift (severe increases in FD and MMD) and noticeable drops in prompt adherence (CLAP), suggesting limited robustness outside synthetic datasets.
